How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

developed a popular estimation approach for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, using simulations to evaluate the performance of two computationally efficient ways to obtain intervals for the indirect effect. While the model can be estimated in a variety of software packages, support in R lags behind as the original approaches to interval estimation were demonstrated using commercial software. Recent research with R instead has only demonstrated interval estimation with more computationally intensive methods.

Meanwhile, other recent work has focused attention towards how Monte Carlo simulation studies are conducted and reported, highlighting the importance of replicating previous findings. Our goals in this manuscript are twofold. First, we show how to implement the original computationally efficient interval estimation methods for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R. We do so by using the Delta method to obtain elements of the asymptotic covariance matrix among model parameters necessary for these approaches. Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate and extend the original simulation study by Bauer et al. (2006). In general, our results indicate that our implementation is operating as expected as Type I error rates and coverage were acceptable when assumptions were met. Furthermore, though we observed higher convergence rates, the major findings from Bauer et al. (2006) were replicated. We hope that extensions to this work will help lead to more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models being readily available to applied researchers.

Introduction

For estimating indirect effects with nested data where all variables are manipulated or measured at the lowest level, the 1-1-1 mediation analysis model is a well-known solution (Krull & MacKinnon, 2001). For instance, in experimental research with repeated measures, the predictor is manipulated on a trial-by-trial basis with the mediator and outcome variables also measured at the same time points. When this model is used and the paths of interest also include random effects, special care must be taken as the indirect effect includes both a product of two coefficients as well as a covariance term among random effects (Kenny et al., 2003). Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006) proposed a solution to estimating all coefficients and the relevant covariance term simultaneously. This approach involved restructuring the data and estimating a single model that predicted both the mediator and outcome variables. Along with their insight into this modeling strategy, Bauer et al. (2006) also proposed two solutions to obtaining confidence intervals for the indirect effect: 1) An approximation assuming an asymptotically normal sampling distribution; and 2) Use of the so-called Monte Carlo method to obtain an approximation to the sampling distribution. Both require an estimate of the asymptotic covariance matrix among the parameter estimates. These approaches were then evaluated in a simulation study and were shown to perform well, but encounter some difficulty under small sample sizes or violation of distributional assumptions.

Despite the original paper being published 20+ years ago, the interval estimation approaches from Bauer et al. (2006) have not been readily available in R (R Core Team, 2025).

The original implementation was in SAS and the authors provided supplementary information on use of other software packages (Mathiowetz & Bauer, 2008a , 2008b). We conjecture that R support was not available because: 1) The lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015), while popular, cannot easily model heteroscedasticity (i.e., different error variances) for the mediator and outcome variables simultaneously; and 2) Other packages such as nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2021) or the newer glmmTMB package (Brooks et al., 2017; McGillycuddy et al., 2025) can estimate the model, but do not provide the components of the asymptotic covariance matrix in a format easily used by applied researchersfoot_0 . An important exception using lme4 was recently provided by Bogaert et al (2025), though after our study was pre-registered and conducted. We return to this paper in the Discussion.

Researchers instead concentrated their efforts on more computationally intensive approaches. For instance, Vuorre & Bolger (2018) developed the bmlm package (Vuorre, 2023), capable of estimating the 1-1-1 model using Bayesian methods and custom Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) code. Falk et al. (2024a) evaluated resampling approaches (i.e., case resampling and a residual-based bootstrap) along with Bayesian estimation using brms (Bürkner, 2017), later developing the multilevelmediation package (Falk et al., 2024b). However, these approaches are sometimes extremely slow or require additional training (e.g., on the use of Bayesian statistics), and at the time of writing bmlm did not support the inclusion of additional covariates. Therefore, one main contribution of this manuscript is to show how intervals for the indirect effect in the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model can be obtained using computationally efficient approaches from Bauer et al. (2006) in conjunction with glmmTMB (Brooks et al., 2017; McGillycuddy et al., 2025) in R.

There have also been recent calls for improving the design and reporting of simulation studies (Siepe et al., 2024) along with high-profile attempts at replicating influential or representative simulation studies (Fairchild et al., 2024; Luijken et al., 2024). In reflecting on the original Bauer et al. (2006) article and this recent work, we note that only a description was provided without full code for the entire simulation study, which some imply could make the study difficult to replicate (Luijken et al., 2024). Furthermore, likely due to computational demands at the time, 500 replications per cell of the simulation may be critiqued by some (e.g., Siepe et al., 2024) as leading to imprecise estimates of Type I error or confidence interval coverage rates upon which the main conclusions were based. In addition, Bauer et al. (2006) included some conditions with nonnormality, yet recent work notes that the generalizability and replicability of prior simulations may depend on the type of nonnormal data generation (Fairchild et al., 2024). Therefore, an additional main contribution of this manuscript is to attempt a partial replication of Bauer et al. (2006) with a pre-registered study. We do so under the additional challenge of evaluating the performance of our own custom R code.

In the remainder of this manuscript, we first introduce the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model and the confidence interval estimation methods used by Bauer et al. (2006). We then show how the necessary pieces of these interval estimation methods can be obtained under the parameterization used by glmmTMB (McGillycuddy et al., 2025). Next, we provide the methods and results of the simulation study, reflecting on similarities and differences with that of Bauer et al. (2006). Finally, we provide concluding remarks.

The 1-1-1 Multilevel Mediation Model and Interval Estimation Techniques

Model Definition

We index clusters (Level 2 units) by 𝑗 = 1, … , 𝑛 2 and observations (Level 1 units) by 𝑖 = 1, … , 𝑛 1 . For instance, clusters may serve as 𝑛 2 participants with each receiving 𝑛 1 trials in an experimental design. Although the model could be set up using two separate equations for the mediator, 𝑀 𝑖𝑗 , and outcome, 𝑌 𝑖𝑗 , this two-equation approach does not allow us to estimate covariances among random effects across such equations. Instead, we follow Bauer et al.'s (2006) approach and stack the mediator (𝑀 𝑖𝑗 ) and outcome (𝑌 𝑖𝑗 ) into a single outcome variable 𝑍 𝑖𝑗 and use indicators to distinguish between them. This allows us to estimate all coefficients and random effect (co)variances simultaneously as part of a single model: In the model specified above, each coefficient has an accompanying random effect, and the random effects are assumed multivariate normal: 𝚺 = [ 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 2 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 ,𝑣 0𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 0𝑗 2 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 ,𝑢 1𝑗 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 0𝑗 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 2 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 0𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 2𝑗 2 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 ,𝑣 1𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 0𝑗 ,𝑣 1𝑗 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 1𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 𝜎 𝑣 1𝑗 2 ]

The above indicates that the means of the random effects are zero (the vector 𝟎), and 𝚺 is the covariance matrix among the random effects. The order of appearance of the random effects in the above matrix is somewhat arbitrary, but corresponds to the order we used in the specified models; later we will see that this matters for how the software estimates the elements in 𝚺. Of particular interest is the covariance between the random effects for the "a" (𝑎 1𝑗 ) and "b" (𝑏 2𝑗 ) paths, or between 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 , which is denoted 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 . This term is required to compute the indirect (mediated) effect under this model (Bauer et al., 2006; Kenny et al., 2003):

To our knowledge and in R, the above model can be properly estimated in a frequentist framework using nlme (Pinheiro et al., 2021) or glmmTMB (McGillycuddy et al., 2025; cf. Bogaert et al., 2025). We next turn to methods to obtain an interval for the indirect effect in (9).

Studied Interval Estimation Techniques

Performing inference or interval estimation for the indirect effect typically requires some way of approximating its sampling distribution. Putting computationally intensive methods aside, both the Monte Carlo method and an asymptotic normal approximation could be employed to obtain confidence intervals for the indirect effect (e.g., MacKinnon et al., 2004). These approaches were introduced and studied for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model by Bauer et al. (2006) and are the focus of the present manuscript.

The asymptotic normal approximation results as a byproduct of using maximum likelihood estimation. The indirect effect is a function of the maximum likelihood estimates of other model parameters. As such, its sampling distribution can also be assumed asymptotically normal and an estimate of its sampling variance can be obtained from elements of an estimate of the so-called asymptotic covariance matrix (ACM) of the model parameters. In brief, the ACM is a q by q matrix, 𝛀, where q is the number of model parameters (e.g., including fixed effect estimates, Level 1 error variances, and random effect variances and covariances); the diagonals of this matrix provide the sampling variability (and their square roots, standard errors) for all model parameters. Across repeated samples, parameter estimates may also tend to co-vary. Thus, the off-diagonal elements are the covariances among model parameters. Bauer et al. (2006) derive an estimate of the sampling variability of the indirect effect by use of a second-order Delta method in conjunction with elements from 𝛀 (p. 147; Eq 9), which under our notation is:

From 𝛀, 𝑉𝑎𝑟(𝑎 ̂1) and 𝑉𝑎𝑟(𝑏 ̂2) represent the sampling variance for estimates of 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 , respectively, 𝑉𝑎𝑟 (𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) is the sampling variance for estimates of 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 , and 𝐶𝑜𝑣(𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2) is the covariance between estimates of 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 . In practice, sample estimates of the parameters (𝑎 ̂1 and 𝑏 ̂2) are substituted into (10) as are elements of an estimated ACM, 𝛀 ̂, yielding, 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑏 ̂2), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), and 𝐶𝑜𝑣 ̂(𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2). The square root of an estimate of (10), 𝑠𝑒 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) = √𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), can then be used to form a confidence interval (CI) for the indirect effect. For example, a 95% CI is formed by: (𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) ± 1.96 × 𝑠𝑒 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ).

The Monte Carlo method leverages theory that parameter estimates are asymptotically multivariate normal, with the best estimate of the means and (co)variances for this distribution given by the respective parameter estimates and estimated ACM, 𝛀 ̂, respectively. Under Bauer et al. (2006), and following example R code from Preacher & Selig (2010), only the subset of parameters composing the indirect effect need to be considered, which reduces tofoot_1 :

Thus, 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 are bivariate normal and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 is normal but independent. The Monte Carlo method then draws the components of the indirect effect from these distributions a large number of times (50,000 for the current study), the indirect effect in (9) is computed for each draw, and the resulting distribution for the indirect effect is used to form a CI (e.g., using the lower and upper 2.5% of the distribution for a 95% CI). However, this approach does not assume that the sampling distribution for the indirect effect itself is normal.

Parameterization of glmmTMB

While glmmTMB (McGillycuddy et al., 2025) readily prints estimates of 𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2, and 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 necessary for either CI method just described, not all elements of the ACM are readily available. Specifically, 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑏 ̂2), and 𝐶𝑜𝑣 ̂(𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2) can be obtained directly, but 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) is not due to how 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 is parameterized. We first describe how 𝚺, and therefore 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 is actually represented, followed by how 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) can then be obtained. This first section requires some knowledge of matrix algebra (e.g., Schott, 2005).

Without loss of generality, under the current model 𝚺 is a 5 × 5 covariance matrix with 5(5 + 1)/2 = 15 unique elements. These parameters are indirectly represented in a vector, 𝜽 = [𝜃 1 𝜃 2 ⋯ 𝜃 15 ]′. The first 5 elements are the log of the random effect standard deviations, 𝝈 = [exp(𝜃 1 ) exp(𝜃 2 ) exp(𝜃 3 ) exp(𝜃 4 ) exp(𝜃 5 )]′ = [ 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗 𝜎 𝜈 0𝑗 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝜎 𝜈 2𝑗 𝜎 𝜈 1𝑗 ]′ . The remaining parameters indirectly represent the correlations among random effects. Let, 𝑳 be an upper triangular matrix of a Cholesky decomposition of this scaled correlation matrix: 𝑳 = [ 1 𝜃 6 𝜃 7 𝜃 9 𝜃 12 0 1 𝜃 8 𝜃 10 𝜃 13 0 0 1 𝜃 11 𝜃 14 0 0 0 1 𝜃 15

The correlation matrix among random effects can then be obtained by: where 𝑫 is a diagonal matrix that rescales 𝑳 ′ 𝑳 to have ones on the diagonal (i.e., 𝑫 is constructed from the inverses of the square root of the diagonal elements of 𝑳 ′ 𝑳).

Then, to obtain 𝚺 we can rescale using the standard deviations of the random effects: where 𝑫 𝝈 is a diagonal matrix with the elements of 𝝈 on the diagonal.

Due to space we do not write all elements of the resulting matrix, but note that 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 can be obtained from ( 15) by:

The desired covariance term, 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 , is thus a function, 𝑔(𝜽), of 𝜃 3 , 𝜃 4 , 𝜃 7 , 𝜃 8 , 𝜃 9 , 𝜃 10 , and 𝜃 11.

To obtain an estimate, 𝑔(𝜽 ̂) = 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 , estimates of these parameters are substituted into (16).

We note that computation of 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 is not invariant to the order in which the random effects are represented in the definition of the model in ( 7) and ( 8). That is, if the random effects are entered into the model in a different order, then glmmTMB will use a different set of parameters to estimate 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 and the expression may look more or less complicated than that in (16). Despite this, writing the effects in a different order would constitute an equivalent model and there is no reason to expect a different final estimate nor any difference in the performance of the resulting standard errors.

Elements of the Asymptotic Covariance Matrix

For the model represented above and in glmmTMB, 𝛀 ̂ (i.e., obtained using vcov() with the model and full=TRUE as arguments) contains an estimate of the sampling variability among the fixed effects, Level 1 error variances, and elements of 𝜽, in that order. 3 Thus, 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑏 ̂2), and 𝐶𝑜𝑣 ̂(𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2) can directly be obtained from this output just by appropriate indexing. To obtain 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), consider just the submatrix of the asymptotic covariances among 𝜽:

Recall that 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 is a function, 𝑔(𝜽), of just the parameters in 𝜽. Using this relation and the first-order Delta method, we can also obtain an approximation to 𝑉𝑎𝑟(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) by: where 𝚫(𝜽) is a Jacobian matrix that contains first-order derivatives of 𝑔(𝜽) with respect to each element of 𝜽, and 𝚫(𝜽 ̂) evaluates this matrix at the estimates, 𝜽 ̂.

Also, since some elements of ( 19) will be zero, some rows and columns of 𝛀 ̂𝜽 need not be considered. While analytical formulae could be used for ( 19), we opted for numerical derivatives using the numDeriv package (Gilbert & Varadhan, 2019) as an initial test rather than programming analytical derivatives. Finally, having obtained an estimate for 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), all components necessary for the asymptotic normal approximation or Monte Carlo method for the indirect effect interval are available.

Method

We next turn to a simulation study to partially replicate Bauer et al. (2006) using our custom R code. The procedure, including simulation conditions, parameter values, and methods applied, followed that of Bauer et al. (2006) as closely as possible, with a few differences.

Data Generation

Consistent with Bauer et al. (2006), our study manipulated the magnitude of the indirect effect, the total sample size, and the distributions from which the random effects were generated.

Some conditions included a non-null indirect effect, while others included a null indirect effect in order to test Type I error rates. Within non-null conditions, the simulation study followed a fully factorial design, consisting of 4 (Level 2 sample size) x 3 (Level 1 sample size) x 2 (Magnitude of fixed effects 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 ) x 3 (Magnitude of 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 ) x 3 (Distribution of 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 ), resulting in 216 non-null simulation conditions (Table 1). The first two factors manipulated sample size by varying either the number of Level 2 units (𝑛2 = 25, 50, 100, or 200) or Level 1 units per cluster (𝑛1 = 4, 8, or 16). The next two factors manipulated the size of the indirect effect by varying either 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 or 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 , which we will describe shortly. In addition to the non-null conditions above, we included additional null conditions designed to test Type I error rates, in which the magnitudes of 𝑎 1 , 𝑏 2 , and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 were fixed to 0, but in which we fully crossed 4 (Level 2 sample size) x 3 (Level 1 sample size) x 3 (distributional conditions) in the same manner as in non-null conditions, resulting in 36 null conditions. In the next two subsections we will elaborate on parameter values as well as the distribution of 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗.

Parameter Values

Population parameter values for the fixed effects were selected to match those used by Bauer et al. (2006). The fixed effects for the causal pathways in the multilevel mediation model were set to the following values: 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0, 0.3, or 0.6 (depending on the condition), and 𝑏1 = 0.2. The fixed intercept for M was 𝑎0 = 0 and the fixed intercept for Y was 𝑏0 = 0.

Values for the random effect variances and covariances were selected to match Bauer et al. (2006). The random slope variance for the 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 paths was 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗2 = 𝜎 𝑣 2𝑗2 = 0.16. The random slope variance for the 𝑏 1 path was 𝜎 𝑣 1𝑗2 = 0.04. The random intercept variance for M was 𝜎 𝑢 0𝑗2 = 0.6 and the random intercept variance for Y was 𝜎 𝑣 0𝑗2 = 0.4. The covariance between the random effects 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 was set to 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 = -0.113, 0, or 0.113, depending on the condition.

All other covariances between random effects were set to 0. In the next section, we describe how the random effects were obtained based on the manipulated distribution of the random effects. Note that to generate the predictor 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 , Bauer et al. (2006) also assumed this variable varied both between and within clusters. Therefore, the predictor 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 was simulated from the equation 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 = 𝑋 ̅ 𝑗 + 𝑒 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 , where 𝑋 ̅ 𝑗 was the cluster-specific deviation from the grand mean (set to 0). One value of 𝑋 ̅ 𝑗 was generated per cluster from a standard normal distribution. The residual component 𝑒 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 was generated separately for each observation also from a standard normal distribution.

Random effect distribution

Manipulation of the distribution for random effects (𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 ) included a normality condition and two nonnormal conditions. Under normality, we simultaneously generated all five random effects from the same multivariate normal distribution in Equation ( 8 . Recall that 𝑋 ̅ 𝑗 is a cluster-specific mean of 𝑋 𝑖𝑗 for cluster j, and has a target variance of 1 and zero covariance with all other random effects. The columns corresponding to 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 were drawn from a chisquared distribution with 3 df, and using the theoretical mean (df) and variance (2df) were then standardized. Other columns were drawn from a standard normal distribution. Then, let 𝑳 ̃ be an upper triangular matrix from a Cholesky decomposition of 𝚺 ̃= 𝑳 ̃′𝑳 ̃, where 𝚺 ̃ is the covariance matrix among random effects, 𝚺, with an additional first column and row prepended due to 𝑋 ̅ 𝑗.

The random effects for the sample are then obtained by the transformation 𝒁𝑳 ̃. In the original paper, it was stated that the desired marginal distribution for these random effects was skew = 1.63 and (excess) kurtosis = 4. It is now known that a Cholesky root transformation is not guaranteed to maintain this marginal distribution for these two random effects. That said, the original procedure still resulted in nonnormality for both of these random effects while maintaining the desired covariance, 𝚺. See Tables A1-A4 in the Supplementary Materials for more details on target and obtained skew and kurtosis.

The second nonnormality condition, not present in Bauer et al. (2006), used the independent generator method (rIG) from the covsim package (version 1.1.0; Grønneberg, et al., 2022), with the latest default settings (method = "triang"), to produce challenging nonnormal data (e.g., see Fairchild et al., 2024). We attempted marginal skew = |2| and excess kurtosis = 5 for 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 , with skew = 0 and excess kurtosis = 0 for other variables. While we preregistered a target skewness of 2 for 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 (which was used in most conditions), when the covariance was negative, we needed to use a skewness value of -2 for the random effect 𝑣 2𝑗 to be able to successfully generate the data. Our chosen skewness and kurtosis values are similar to, but not exactly the same, as values often used in robustness studies (e.g., skew = 2 and kurtosis = 7; Curran et al., 1996; Falk, 2018), as the IG method is now somewhat known for being quite challenging (e.g., Chen et al., 2024).

Estimation and Software

Estimation was conducted in R version 4.5.0 (R Core Team, 2025). We fit the model using the multilevelmediation package in R (version 0.4.1; Falk et al., 2024b) which stacks 𝑀 𝑖𝑗 and 𝑌 𝑖𝑗 into a single column 𝑍 𝑖𝑗 and uses the unified Equation ( 1); all random effects were estimated. This package acts as a wrapper for the glmmTMB package (version 1.1.11; Brooks et al., 2017; McGillycuddy et al., 2025). We used restricted maximum likelihood (REML), the optim optimizer with BFGS, and increased the maximum number of iterations to 1000. These additional settings were selected to match those used by Bauer et al. (2006). While we preregistered the use of the optim optimizer, we decided to automatically try the nlminb optimizer if the model failed to converge with optim. This modification improved convergence and resulted in a greater number of useable replications. To facilitate replicability, the complete output of devtools::session_info()is reported in the Supplementary Materials.

We applied two methods for constructing 95% CIs for the indirect effect to each replication: the asymptotic normal approximation method and the Monte Carlo method with 50,000 random draws. In their original study, Bauer et al. (2006) applied two different methods to extract the ACM of the fixed effect estimates: the "standard" method and the Kackar-Harville (K-H) method (Kackar & Harville, 1984). The standard method derives the ACM by taking the inverse of the information matrix for the estimates. According to Bauer et al. (2006), in multilevel models (likely with small samples), this method tends to underestimate the sampling variability of the fixed effect estimates. The K-H method adjusts for the underestimation bias by inflating the elements of the ACM. Because the K-H method is not readily available with glmmTMB, we only used the standard method to extract the ACM in this study.

As outlined in the introduction, since not all elements of the ACM are provided directly by glmmTMB, custom code by the first author was used to obtain the missing element, in part using numDeriv (version 2016.8-1.1; Gilbert & Varadhan, 2019) for numerical derivatives.

Otherwise, the asymptotic normal approximation used Equation ( 10) and code from Preacher and Selig (2010) was modified for the Monte Carlo method.

Outcomes of Interest

We assessed convergence rates under different simulation conditions and the bias of the indirect effect and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 estimates. Then, we compared the performance of both indirect effect CI methods in terms of Type I error rates, CI coverage, and power. Convergence was considered successful when the optimizer returned a convergence code of 0, the Hessian matrix was positive definite, the smallest eigenvalue of the estimated covariance matrix was positive, and both the asymptotic normal approximation and Monte Carlo CIs could be computed. Bias was computed as the difference between the mean estimate across all replications within a given condition and the corresponding true population value. The Type I error rate was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs for the average indirect effect failed to contain zero under conditions where the indirect effect was null. We compared the observed Type I error rate to the nominal alpha level of 0.05. Coverage was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs contained the true value of the indirect effect. Note that Type I error and coverage are redundant in null conditions. As a benchmark, coverage and Type I error also used Bradley's liberal criterion (Bradley, 1978): For a nominal alpha level of 5%, acceptable Type I error rates should fall between 2.5% and 7.5%, and for 95% coverage, between 92.5% and 97.5%. Power was calculated for the main design cells where the true indirect effect was not zero.

In addition, our pre-registration specified that we would aim for a qualitative assessment of whether our results replicated that of Bauer et al. (2006), comparing both sets of results for coverage and Type I error to Bradley's criterion and noting that: … the main findings should be that 1) estimation problems are abundant at small sample sizes, with only 𝑛1 = 16 and 𝑛 2 > 25, or 𝑛1 = 8 and 𝑛2 = 200 having more than 90% unconstrained solutions; 2) Type I error rates should be calibrated for both CI methods under most conditions, with the smallest sample sizes providing some challenge, and non-normality providing an additional challenge; 3) The CIs should have well calibrated coverage rates, except when non-normal random effects are present, with coverage rates dropping to around 90%; these authors also report coverage being worse when the covariance between the random effects was non-zero (especially 0.113).

Results

The following sections detail our results for difficulty of estimation, bias, Type I error, CI coverage, and power, and compare the observed patterns to those reported by Bauer et al. (2006).

Within each section, as specified in our study's pre-registration, we will first present the full, uncollapsed results across all conditions and describe the observed patterns. In addition, because one of the goals of our study was the partial replication of Bauer et al. (2006), we will also show figures collapsed across the same conditions in the same layout as the original paper to enable easier comparison between the two sets of findings.

Difficulty of Estimation

Prior to the examination of performance measures, we first assessed the difficulty of estimation by examining convergence rates across all simulation conditions (Figure 1). Overall, convergence rates were high (e.g., near .8 or higher) except at the combination of the lowest Level 1 and 2 sample size. In addition, there seemed to be a small effect of the random effect covariance, 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 , population value on convergence rates, such that when the population covariance was zero, convergence rates were higher than when it was non-zero. Only unproblematic solutions were included in evaluations of subsequent performance measures.

In their paper, Bauer et al. (2006, Table 1, p. 150) presented a table of convergence rates as a function of 𝑛 1 and 𝑛 2 , collapsing across all other conditions. Figure 2 reproduces the format of this table as closely as possible. Overall, our study produced higher convergence rates than Bauer et al. (2006). For example, while Bauer et al. (2006) reported 20.27% unproblematic solutions when 𝑛2 = 25 and 𝑛1 = 8, our study produced 80.59% unproblematic solutions at the same sample size combination. Bauer et al. (2006) also found that the model became more stable when there were more

Level 1 units at the expense of Level 2 units, suggesting that the two sample size factors did not exert an equal influence on convergence. For example, with a fixed overall sample size of 800 observations, they found that convergence was 87.23% with 𝑛1 = 8 and 𝑛2 = 100. However, when the number of Level 1 units was increased to 𝑛1 = 16 at the expense of Level 2 units, decreased to 𝑛2 = 50, convergence increased to 92.10%. We did not find a similar pattern in our study, perhaps because convergence rates at larger sample sizes were already very high. Indeed, using these same sample size combinations, convergence was 99.53% when 𝑛1 = 8 and 𝑛2 = 100, and 99.31% when 𝑛 1 was increased to 16 and 𝑛 2 was decreased to 50.

In examining collapsing across some conditions, Bauer et al. (2006) also reported three small effects of other factors. First, they observed better convergence with normally distributed random effects. We found a similar pattern: normally distributed random effects produced an average convergence rate of 92.41%, compared to 91.52% for nonnormally distributed random effects. Second, they observed better convergence when the values of 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 were smaller (0.3). Likewise, we found slightly better average convergence when 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 were 0.3 (92.06%) compared to 0.6 (91.00%). Third, they found better convergence when the covariance between random effects was zero. Similarly, in our study, average convergence was 93.10% when the covariance was zero and 90.85% when the covariance was non-zero.

Bias of the Estimates

The indirect effect estimates were generally unbiased, and the level of bias was comparable to, if not smaller than, that reported by Bauer et al. (2006). In our study, the mean bias of the indirect effect was -0.0001 (compared to -0.001 in Bauer et al. (2006)), the minimum bias was -0.017 (compared to -0.076 in Bauer et al. (2006)), and the maximum bias was 0.021 (compared to 0.027 in Bauer et al. (2006)).

Furthermore, in our study, the absolute bias was smaller than 0.01 in all but eight conditions, all of which involved nonnormal random effects, and six of which had the smallest Level 1 sample size of four. This result is consistent with Bauer et al. (2006), who also reported that absolute bias above 0.01 occurred mostly under nonnormal and small sample size conditions. Figure C1 (see Supplementary Materials) shows the bias of the indirect effect estimate for all 252 simulation conditions, with conditions in which absolute bias exceeded 0.01 colored in red.

Consistent with Bauer et al. (2006), we also computed the bias of the covariance estimate for the random effects 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 . The covariance estimate was generally unbiased, and absolute bias levels were smaller than those reported by Bauer et al. (2006). In our study, the mean bias for the covariance estimate was -0.0000047 (compared to 0.0002 in Bauer et al. (2006)), the minimum bias was -0.010 (compared to 0.033 in Bauer et al. (2006)), and the maximum bias was 0.013 (compared to 0.041 in Bauer et al. (2006)). Moreover, the absolute bias was smaller than 0.01 in all the conditions except one. This condition involved nonnormally distributed random effects and the smallest Level 1 sample size. Figure C2 (see Supplementary Materials) shows the bias of the covariance estimate for all 252 conditions, with the condition in which absolute bias exceeded 0.01 colored in red.

In sum, we did not observe substantial bias in either the indirect effect or covariance estimates. Our study seemed to produce smaller absolute bias levels than Bauer et al. (2006), perhaps due to the larger number of replications. Similar to Bauer et al. (2006), cases in which absolute bias exceeded 0.01 occurred mostly under nonnormal and small sample size conditions.

Type I Error Rates

Next, we investigated Type I error rates using the 36 additional conditions in which the true indirect effect was set to zero. Type I Error Rates Across All Null Conditions Note. NA = Normal approximation; MC = Monte Carlo method. Bolded cells with an asterisk indicate a Type I error rate outside of Bradley's liberal criterion.

Overall, Type I error rates tended to fall below the nominal 5% level, especially when the NA method was used. All but 10/72 conditions had a Type I error rate within Bradley's acceptable range. The 10 conditions outside the range fell below the 2.5% cutoff, indicating overly conservative Type I error rates, and occurred at the smallest Level 2 sample size of 25. In addition, 7/10 of these conditions involved CIs constructed using the NA method, suggesting that the MC method was better at reflecting the nominal Type I error rate at small sample sizes.

In their paper, Bauer et al. (2006) presented two tables summarizing Type I error rates as a function of 𝑛 1 , 𝑛 2 , and CI method. One table showed results for normal random effects (Table 2, p. 151) and the other, for chi-squared (nonnormal) random effects (Table 3, p. 152). Figures 3A and 3B already reproduce the format of these tables as closely as possible. We observed Type I error rates that were broadly comparable to those reported by Bauer et al. (2006). Across the 48 cells shown in Figures 3A and 3B, approximately half were closer to the nominal level in Bauer et al. (2006), whereas the remaining half were closer in our study. In addition, 9/48 cells fell outside of Bradley's range in Bauer et al. (2006), compared to 7/48 in our study, all under smaller sample sizes. Six of these seven conditions were also outside of Bradley's criterion in Bauer et al. (2006), indicating a high overlap in the conditions with problematic Type I error rates; the remaining 𝑛2 = 8, 𝑛1 = 25 condition under normality may have been within Bradley's criterion in Bauer et al. (2006) in part due to lower convergence rates or just sampling variability as the Type I error rate was .0297 in their study and .0210 in ours. Beyond our study, Bauer et al. (2006) also had 𝑛2 = 4 and 𝑛1 = 50 with chi-square nonnormality as having low Type I error rates for both methods that were outside of Bradey's criterion, though these were within the expected limit under our study. We did not, therefore, notice Type I error rates that were more problematic for nonnormal data. However, note that under the problematic conditions Bauer et al. (2006) also experienced more corresponding convergence problems. Bauer et al. (2006) found that both CI methods tended to produce Type I error rates below the nominal level of 5%. We observed the same pattern: only 4/48 cells in Figures 3A and 3B exceeded 5% (compared to 10/48 in Bauer et al. (2006)), though none in either study were outside of Bradley's criterion. Moreover, Bauer et al. (2006) found that CIs constructed using the MC method more closely reflected the nominal 5% level than those constructed using the NA method. Similarly, we found that out of the 24 possible comparisons in Figures 3A and 3B, the NA method outperformed the MC method only in three cases (compared to four cases in Bauer et al. (2006)).

Confidence Interval Coverage Rates

Next, we investigated CI coverage rates. Figure 4 displays NA and MC CI coverage rates across all conditions with coverage rates falling outside Bradley's acceptable range bolded with an asterisk. Overall, the NA method and the MC method both produced coverage rates close to the nominal rate when the random effects were normally distributed. However, both methods experienced difficulty producing robust coverage rates when the random effects were nonnormally distributed, especially when the covariance was positive and, to a lesser extent, when it was negative. These difficulties did not emerge when the covariance was zero. Indeed, when the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was positive, all 96 cells in that section of the design fell below Bradley's lower limit of 92.5% coverage. When the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was negative, 36/96 of the cells exhibited undercoverage and fell below Bradley's lower limit. In contrast, when the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was zero, only 7/96 of the cells fell outside Bradley's range, including six cases of under-coverage and one case of over-coverage, all occurring at the smallest Level 2 sample size of 25. Finally, regardless of the covariance value, when the random effects were normally distributed, only 3/144 cells were outside of Bradley's criterion, including one case of under-coverage and two cases of over-coverage, all at 𝑛2 = 25. CI Coverage Rates Across All Conditions Note. NA = Normal approximation; MC = Monte Carlo method. Bolded cells with an asterisk indicate a CI coverage rate outside of Bradley's liberal criterion. Bauer et al. (2006) reported that the distribution of the random effects was the factor that exerted the most influence on coverage rates and that coverage rates were least affected by nonnormality when the covariance was zero: findings which our study replicated. Overall, the coverage rates obtained in our study were comparable to those reported by Bauer et al. (2006), although they were just slightly higher. For example, Bauer et al. (2006) obtained an average coverage across all conditions of about 94% with normal random effects and about 90% with nonnormal random effects (p. 151), while we obtained an average coverage across all conditions of about 95% and 91%, respectively.

The authors of the original study asserted that the obtained CIs tended to be too narrow, except at the smallest sample size combination with normal random effects, where the CIs were too wide. Presumably, given unbiased point estimates, narrow intervals correspond to undercoverage and wide intervals correspond to over-coverage. In examining Figure 4, we observed a similar pattern: the widest CIs (over-coverage) in our study also occurred at the smallest sample size combination with normal random effects, whereas the CIs were generally too narrow (undercoverage) under other conditions. In addition, Bauer et al. (2006) reported a slight advantage of the NA method over the MC method. Collapsing across all conditions, we found that the NA method (92.38% coverage) performed almost the same as the MC method (92.17% coverage).

Finally, Bauer et al. (2006) reported slightly better coverage at smaller sample sizes, which we also observed. Collapsing across all other conditions, coverage decreased by minute amounts as sample sizes increased: coverage was 93.33% with 𝑛1 = 4; 92.25% with 𝑛1 = 8; and 91.24% with 𝑛1 = 16 and it was 92.54% with 𝑛2 = 25; 92.29% with 𝑛2 = 50; 92.20% with 𝑛2 = 100; and 92.07% with 𝑛2 = 200.

Consistent with the tables presented in Bauer et al. (2006), we provide results of coverage rates by sample size (Figure 5; Table 4, p. 153 in Bauer et al., 2006) and by the magnitude of the population parameters (Figure 6; Table 5, p. 154 in Bauer et al., 2006). Coverage Rates as a Function of Random Effect Distribution, 𝑛 1 , 𝑛 2 , and CI Method Note. NA = Normal approximation; MC = Monte Carlo method. Bolded cells with an asterisk indicate a CI coverage rate outside of Bradley's liberal criterion.

In Figure 5, 18/48 cells exceeded the lower bound of Bradley's criterion, compared to 22/48 cells in Table 4 (p.153) of Bauer et al. (2006). The 18 conditions that fell outside Bradley's criterion in our study were also outside the range in Bauer et al. (2006), indicating a high overlap in conditions with problematic CI coverage rates. All 18 of these conditions involved nonnormal random effects. Bauer et al. (2006) reported four additional conditions that fell outside Bradley's criterion but remained within the acceptable range in our study. These four conditions also involved nonnormal random effects and all occurred at the smallest Level 1 sample size (𝑛1 = 4).

Specifically, these conditions corresponded to 𝑛2 = 25 with the MC method, 𝑛2 = 50 with the NA and MC methods, and 𝑛2 = 100 with the NA method. Coverage Rates as a Function of Random Effect Distribution, Parameter Values, and CI Method Note. NA = Normal approximation; MC = Monte Carlo method. Bolded cells with an asterisk indicate a CI coverage rate outside of Bradley's liberal criterion.

In Figure 6, 6/24 cells exceeded the lower bound of Bradley's criterion, compared to 8/24 cells in Table 5 (p.154) of Bauer et al. (2006). All 6 conditions that fell outside Bradley's criterion in our study also fell outside the criterion in Bauer et al. (2006), once again indicating a high overlap in conditions with problematic CI coverage rates. These 6 conditions all involved nonnormal random effects and non-zero covariance. In both studies, under nonnormal random effects and regardless of the population values of 𝑎1 = 𝑏 2 , coverage was poor when the covariance was positive and acceptable when the covariance was zero. The only discrepancy occurred when the covariance was negative: Bauer et al. (2006) reported inadequate coverage for both 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.3 and 0.6, whereas in our study, inadequate coverage occurred only when 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.3. Overall, coverage was most affected by nonnormality when the covariance was positive and not affected when the covariance was zero, which is consistent with Bauer et al. (2006) and our anticipated results. Coverage was slightly worse under the combination of nonnormality and a negative covariance under Bauer et al. (2006) than it was in our study.

Power

Finally, Figure 7 displays power rates across all non-null conditions. Not surprisingly, power improved as the magnitude of the true indirect effect became larger. Indeed, when the magnitude of the true indirect effect was at its smallest (𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 = -0.113 and 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.3), power ranged from 1.87% to 28.35%. In contrast, when the magnitude of the true indirect effect was at its largest (𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 = 0.113 and 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.6), power ranged from 94.34% to 100.00%.

Power also improved with increases in sample size: at the smallest sample size combination, average power across conditions was 48.92%, whereas at the largest sample size combination, average power was 87.70%. Across all conditions, the average power was 75.44%. Bauer et al. (2006) reported that the MC method resulted in slightly superior power rates than the NA method and that these differences were small. We observed a similar pattern, with the MC method producing slightly higher power than the NA method. Indeed, out of all the possible comparisons in Figure 7, the MC method outperformed the NA method in 108/216 cases, performed equally to the NA method in 94/216 cases, and performed worse than the NA method in only 14/216 cases. Collapsed across all conditions, the average power under the MC method was 75.82%, compared to 75.06% for the NA method.

Power Across All Conditions

Discussion

Our simulation study had two main goals. First, we aimed to test whether estimating the model using glmmTMB (McGillycuddy et al., 2025) and custom R code for the Delta method to obtain the asymptotic covariance between random effects 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 could be used to produce confidence intervals for the indirect effect in the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation model. This goal was achieved: our study produced reasonable results across the examined performance measures.

Indeed, we obtained high convergence rates; our estimates were largely unbiased; the Type I error rate was often close to the nominal rate, particularly with the Monte Carlo method at larger sample sizes; and power to detect the indirect effect was high when its population magnitude was far from zero. With respect to CI coverage, rates were generally within Bradley's criterion range when the random effects were normally distributed and/or the covariance between the random effects was zero. However, under-coverage occurred under conditions involving nonnormal random effects and, especially, a positive covariance value. Problems also emerged at the smallest sample sizes, and neither method performed particularly well in terms of CI coverage under nonnormality.

Second, we aimed to replicate the simulation study conducted by Bauer et al. (2006) to evaluate the MC and NA methods to generate confidence intervals in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models. Whereas Bauer et al. (2006) conducted their study using SAS PROC MIXED, we conducted ours using open-source software. Following Bauer et al.'s (2006) data generation procedure as closely as possible, we were able to replicate the main patterns reported in their study. Although our performance metrics were slightly better overall, the only notable discrepancy concerned convergence rates being much higher in our study. Luckily, we were able to perform this partial replication without much help from the original authors, we think owing to a simulation study that was well described in the original publication. The small discrepancies in results observed between the two studies may be attributable to a few factors. First, our study used a larger number of replications (2000 replications per cell compared to 500 in Bauer et al. (2006)), and it could be that some deviations are due to sampling variability in Bauer et al.'s (2006) results. Second, we implemented some automated troubleshooting in the case of nonconvergence (which we did not pre-register), and in retrospect it appears that this may have led to a great increase in the number of converged models. 4 Third, other methodological differences could have contributed, including the use of R rather than SAS.

Moreover, because evaluating methods under different forms of simulated nonnormality can lead to different conclusions about their performance (Fairchild et al., 2024), we extended the simulation replication by incorporating an additional method of generating nonnormal data, the IG method (Grønneberg, et al., 2022). Confidence interval coverage was slightly higher under the chi-squared method (the nonnormality method used by Bauer et al. (2006)) than under the IG method; whereas Type I error rates were closer to the nominal level under the IG method than under the chi-squared method, though these differences were generally small. This suggests that performance metrics may differ slightly depending on how nonnormality is generated, but that the original results generalize to an additional type of nonnormality.

In partially replicating Bauer et al. (2006), we did not employ the K-H method to also extract the ACM, which is one of two methods to compute the ACM in their study. This approach may perform better in small samples. However, the method of computing the ACM is embedded in a broader issue of how to handle difficult estimation conditions as well as misspecification (e.g., due to distributional or other assumption violations). Both the NA and the MC methods for constructing CIs in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models were not robust to nonnormal random effects. Indeed, the distribution of the random effects was the factor that exerted the greatest influence on CI coverage rates. When normality assumptions for the multilevel model do not hold (e.g., random effects are not multivariate normal), then the elements of the ACM that are not well approximated. Researchers should proceed with caution, checking normality assumptions of the random effects (e.g., an approximate way to do this is to obtain empirical Bayes estimates of the random effects and then test for univariate and multivariate normality) before proceeding to use the methods studied in this manuscript.

If nonnormality is suspected, alternative approaches such as bootstrapping may provide

CIs that are robust to nonnormality (e.g., Lai, 2021; Vallejo Seco et al., 2013). However, although Falk et al. (2024a) studied such an approach for this particular 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, resampling is computationally intensive and these authors did not study nonnormality. If one adopts a Bayesian estimation approach, there is also hope of adapting infinitesimal jackknife standard errors to obtain robust sampling variability estimates (Ji et al., 2025). In addition, we hope that future research may employ other computationally fast techniques that can provide elements of the ACM using computations that are robust to assumption violations (e.g., Wang & Merkle, 2018); to our knowledge, code for this approach is not yet available for glmmTMB.

Despite both NA and MC underperforming under nonnormality, we proceeded with these methods for several reasons. First, they are far more computationally feasible than resampling and Bayesian approaches; Bauer et al.'s (2006) study might not have been easily replicable otherwise without a computing cluster. Second, sometimes there are potential drawbacks to these more intense methods. Bayesian estimation does not automatically address distributional assumption violations (Falk & Chen, 2026; Ji et al., 2025). Resampling in multilevel models is also not straightforward, especially in the case of an imbalance in the number of Level 1 units per cluster (e.g., Sherman & le Cessie, 1997), though in this situation a residual-based bootstrap may be used (e.g., Falk et al., 2024a; Lai, 2021; van der Leeden et al., 2008). Third, either the asymptotic NA or MC approach are more straightforward to apply in models beyond that considered here, such as within-cluster centering approaches (e.g., Zhang et al., 2009).

Alternatively, Bogaert et al (2025) recently provided an approach that tricks lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) into estimating the 1-1-1 model with heteroscedasticity by means of adding an orthogonal random effect term. This approach then uses the bootmlm package (Lai, 2026) to obtain ACM elements and computes CIs using the Monte Carlo method. The authors demonstrate use of a sandwich covariance that is robust misspecification. This may be preferable to our own approach, yet a direct comparison remains. A potential downside is that lme4 may not allow for certain parameter constraints employed by within-cluster centering that can more easily be done with glmmTMB. Likewise, simplifications to the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model make other approaches easier. If either random effect, 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 , is omitted, then 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 = 0 and the indirect effect reduces to just the product of two fixed effects coefficients, 𝑎 1 𝑏 2 . In such a case, we conjecture that two separate models can be employed, lme4 used for estimation (Bates et al., 2015), and robust standard errors obtained (e.g., Wang & Merkle, 2018) for use with the Monte Carlo method. This approach requires only separate point estimates for 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 , as well as their standard errors. But, Bogaert et al (2025) caution that CI coverage rates deteriorate if non-zero random effects are accidentally omitted from the model.

If using glmmTMB, since there was little difference between the NA and MC method, it is not strictly necessary to employ the Delta method to obtain the desired element of the asymptotic covariance matrix if only the Monte Carlo method is desired. One may alternatively sample all elements of 𝜽 from a multivariate normal distribution with covariances specified by the ACM given by glmmTMB, and transform each set of draws to compute 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 for forming a distribution of the indirect effect.

We also note that the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, as presented, may not be the best model to employ depending on the situation. Our own position is that the present model may be appropriate for either experimental data where the predictor is manipulated and therefore does not vary on average across clusters, or with cross-sectional clustered data where there is an imbalance in the number of Level 1 units and separation of within-and between-cluster effects is not desired. Otherwise, and aside from centering issues already discussed, some researchers may prefer a multilevel structural equation modeling approach (e.g., Preacher et al., 2011 Preacher et al., , 2010)). For purely observational and longitudinal data, one might alternatively consider employing a random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015). The RI-CLPM method separates stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations and could be a useful approach for investigating mediation effects that take time to unfold. In addition, dynamic structural equation models (DSEM; McNeish & Hamaker, 2020) are useful for modelling intensive longitudinal data, where individuals provide a large amount of data over a relatively short interval and could also be used for investigating questions regarding mediated effects.

However, such an approach is cutting-edge and open-source software may be limited.

In conclusion, we developed and tested code for computing confidence intervals in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models and showed that this approach is feasible in R. Despite the replication of simulation studies being relatively rare, researchers have argued that it is an important endeavor. We partially replicated the simulation study conducted by Bauer et al. (2006), who evaluated asymptotic normal approximation and Monte Carlo confidence intervals in SAS, whereas our study was conducted in the free, open-source software R. Overall, our results suggest that the proposed R implementation performs adequately in producing confidence intervals for the indirect effect in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models, and that the main patterns reported by Bauer et al. (2006) can be replicated using an alternative software. We hope that extensions to this work will help make more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models readily available to applied researchers.
